idiom_name: guard early exit + throws for recoverable refusal, precondition()/fatalError() for impossible states
implementation_notes: Swift separates the two fail-fast levels in the language. A throwing function reports a failure the caller can act on (do/try/catch, or try? when the error is deliberately ignored), and guard binds and validates values while exiting the current scope immediately in the else branch, which keeps the success path unindented. On the other side, precondition() checks a necessary condition for making forward progress and traps - in release builds as well - and fatalError() unconditionally prints a message and stops execution, returning Never so the compiler knows the path cannot continue. Use throws where the request can be refused and the process should survive; use the trapping functions only for programmer errors and states that cannot be handled.
pitfalls: assert() is removed in optimized builds while precondition() is not: choosing the debug-only one for a production contract (or the trapping one for user input) silently changes what the app enforces - and can turn a bad request into a crash.
try! and as! are fail-fast without context: the trap message is generic and the whole process dies where a thrown error would have refused just this request.
try? discards the error value, and a catch that ignores its error restores fail-slow behaviour; errors are unchecked, so nothing forces the caller to look.
